strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical insight: the paper convincingly demonstrates (Tab. 1, Fig. 2, Tab. 9) that a strong 'hidden' detector exists inside MOTR and is suppressed by track queries, which is a useful diagnostic for the community working on end-to-end MOT.

Systematic and unusually thorough ablation study: the four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposals) are cleanly isolated and compared (Tab. 2), and the final design choices (proposal source, threshold, HSV/CrowdHuman scaling, denoising, decoder depth) are each individually validated (Tabs. 5-8, Fig. 5).
Competitive results on DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA, best AssA among end-to-end trackers at 59.3) while remaining detector-free, with an explicit runtime analysis showing only ~17% overhead (Tab. 10).
The paper honestly positions itself against MOTRv2-style methods in Sec. 5 and states limitations (only a MOTR-style baseline, only DanceTrack and MOT17).

The demonstration that the detection-association conflict is nearly eliminated in the self-proposal architecture (Tab. 9: AP drop of -0.3 vs -6.3 for MOTR) is a substantive empirical finding supporting the design.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to existing work: the core mechanism (injecting 4D anchor proposals from a detector into MOTR) is essentially MOTRv2, with the delta being that the detector shares weights with the tracker. The paper acknowledges this in Sec. 5 but the contribution is a third point in a known design space rather than a fundamentally new algorithm; CO-MOT also already achieves detector-free end-to-end tracking via shadow queries.

Results do not establish clear state of the art: on DanceTrack test, SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) trails CO-MOT (69.4) and MOTRv2 (69.9), and on MOT17 it falls well behind CO-MOT (57.5 vs 60.1 HOTA) and even MeMOTR (58.8). The MOT17 shortcoming is only lightly justified by the 'detector-free' framing, yet the joint training still uses CrowdHuman pseudo-clips and MOTRv2's QIMv2, weakening the purity claim.

The reported MOTR baseline (51.2 HOTA val, 54.2 test) is below the commonly cited 57-58 for MOTR on DanceTrack, so the relative gains against the baseline may be inflated; a comparison at a stronger baseline (e.g., MOTRv2 configuration) is not provided for the self-proposal mechanism.

The 'fully end-to-end' framing is somewhat strained: the model still performs two decoder passes at inference, and the analysis experiments (Tab. 2) all rely on a separately detection-pretrained, frozen MOTR teacher/generator, which is itself an external model during those experiments.

Theoretical understanding is thin: the paper does not explain why track queries suppress detection (beyond 'competitive interaction'), nor why confidence-modulated proposal queries improve association; mechanism claims rest on correlations in metrics.

Some presentation issues: Table 4's gray-font 'unfair comparison' convention is not rigorously defined; the Discussion contains a grammatically incomplete claim ('indicate the effectiveness of our novel paradigm'); detection precision in the multi-threshold Tab. 1 is labeled 'AP' inconsistently with the mAP discussion; the exploration is confined to one architecture family and the extension to CO-MOT/MOTRv3 is left unstudied, as the authors admit.

strengths: The central empirical observation is interesting and well-motivated: standard MOTR, trained end-to-end, contains a substantially stronger detector than what is exposed during tracking inference (mAP 60.0 -> 66.3 when track queries are disabled, Tab. 1 / Fig. 2). This cleanly reframes the detection-association conflict as a competition/inference issue rather than a representational one.

The paper provides a systematic, well-organized study of four distinct prior-injection mechanisms (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposals) with quantitative evidence for each (Tab. 2), which is a useful contribution to the community beyond the final method itself.

The final method is genuinely detector-free and end-to-end in spirit: self-generated proposals from a shared-weight detection-only pass substitute for the external YOLOX anchors used in MOTRv2, and Tab. 6 shows self proposals match frozen detector-derived anchors without accuracy loss. Tab. 9 provides direct evidence that the detection-association conflict is essentially removed (-0.3 AP vs. -6.3 for MOTR).

Ablations are extensive (successive components, proposal source, data scaling, confidence threshold, decoder depth, runtime), and the runtime analysis (20.7 FPS vs. 24.8 FPS) shows the dual-pass design is practical.

On DanceTrack the method is competitive with the strongest end-to-end trackers (69.2 HOTA, highest AssA 59.3 in the end-to-end block), and the paper honestly attributes the slightly lower DetA to the detector-free setting.
Limitations are stated candidly (only instantiated on MOTR-style baseline; DanceTrack/MOT17 focus; unstudied integration with CO-MOT/MOTRv3).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior work. The core mechanism (feeding 4D anchor proposals into MOTR-style decoding) is essentially the MOTRv2 recipe, with the main change being that proposals come from the model itself rather than an external YOLOX. The paper positions this as a 'third point in the design space' (Sec. 5), which is a fair but modest distinction; the conceptual delta over CO-MOT's shadow queries or MOTRv2's query alignment is limited.

Results on MOT17 are weak: 57.5 HOTA / 70.0 MOTA falls below MOTRv3 (60.2/75.9), CO-MOT (60.1/72.6), and even MeMOTR (58.8/72.8). The justification that stronger methods 'rely on detector-aligned training or stronger external boxes' is unsatisfying for a paper whose headline claim is removing the need for external priors; it suggests the benefit is largely DanceTrack-specific (uniform appearance, where detection is the bottleneck).

There is an unexplained gap between the ablation setup and the reported main results. Tab. 5 ends at 64.4 HOTA on the validation set, yet Tab. 3 reports 69.2 on the test set, and Sec. 4.2 reveals the final model uses the QIMv2 module from MOTRv2. Since QIMv2 is tied to MOTRv2's detector-bootstrapped design, the claimed 'fully detector-free / end-to-end' characterization needs a more careful justification; the experimental bookkeeping across validation/test configurations is confusing.

The method requires a two-stage training pipeline (detection pretraining followed by tracking training) and a double decoder pass at inference, which partially undercuts the simplicity/self-containedness argument used to criticize external-detector approaches; the paper does not quantify the cost of the pretraining stage or compare against a distilled YOLOX-free baseline of equal training budget.

All experiments appear to be single runs without variance or significance estimates, despite several claimed margins being small (e.g., 69.2 vs. 69.4 HOTA on test, 58.2 vs. 58.0 in Tab. 6), making some conclusions fragile.

Clarity issues: the claim that self proposals yield 'the highest association score in the end-to-end block' rests on a 0.4 AssA margin over CO-MOT while HOTA is actually lower; Table 4 mixes 'fair' and 'unfair' (grayed) comparisons that complicate reading; the mechanism for why confidence-modulated content embeddings (q_prop + PE(c)) help is not analyzed.

Generalization of the analysis is untested beyond one architecture family (MOTR) and the stated limitation that integration into CO-MOT/MOTRv3 remains unexplored is significant, since those are the methods SelfMOTR is compared against in Tab. 3.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: the paper empirically demonstrates that MOTR contains a 'hidden' detector (60.0 -> 66.3 mAP when track queries are removed at inference), cleanly dissecting the detection-association conflict in end-to-end trackers.

The systematic study of four prior-injection mechanisms (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposals) in Tab. 2 and Fig. 3 is a genuinely useful contribution for practitioners, going beyond a single proposed method.

SelfMOTR is competitive on DanceTrack (69.2 HOTA, best end-to-end AssA of 59.3, IDF1 72.5) while remaining fully detector-free and end-to-end, directly addressing the main criticism of MOTRv2-style approaches that reintroduce an external detector.

Extensive ablations covering proposal sources, thresholds, data scaling, decoder depth (Fig. 5), detection-association conflict (Tab. 9), and runtime (Tab. 10) provide good evidence and support the design choices; the ~17% FPS overhead is modest and well characterized.
The paper is well organized, and the Discussion and Limitations sections are candid about scope (MOTR-style instantiation only, unstudied integration into CO-MOT/MOTRv3).
weaknesses: Results on MOT17 are weak: SelfMOTR (57.5 HOTA, DetA 57.3) is below MOTRv3, CO-MOT, and even MeMOTR, and its DetA is lower than the original MOTR baseline (60.3). The claim of 'strong performance' essentially rests on DanceTrack alone, and the benchmark breadth is limited.

The headline observation (MOTR's hidden detection capability when track queries are removed) is attributed to prior work [23], which reduces the novelty of the analysis contribution; the remaining novelty is mainly the architectural mechanism of self-generated proposals, which is an incremental step over MOTRv2's external-detector anchor proposals (the internal-vs-external distinction is somewhat narrow, and CO-MOT already explores detector-free query management).

The 'fully end-to-end' framing needs qualification: the method still requires a separate detection-pretrained stage on the target dataset, uses QIMv2 from MOTRv2, and runs two decoder passes; the pipeline is detector-free but not single-pass, which partially blurs the claimed conceptual advantage over external-proposal methods.

The ablation on proposal confidence threshold (Tab. 8) considers only two values (0.05, 0.5), and Fig. 5 is hard to read from its dual-axis plot; several experimental details (e.g., why 10 epochs for DanceTrack but 180 for MOT17) are under-justified.
No explicit statement about code release or reproducibility, and the comparison tables mix fair and 'unfair' (gray) comparisons, which complicates precise positioning against the state of the art.

strengths: Well-motivated empirical study: the observation that MOTR's detection quality improves when track queries are disabled at inference (Fig. 2) is a clean, reproducible diagnostic that directly motivates the method, and the four-way ablation of prior-injection strategies (pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) is thorough and informative to the community.

The proposed SelfMOTR is simple, detector-free, and fully internal: generating proposals from the model's own detection-only pass and reusing them as 4D anchor queries avoids external detectors (MOTRv2/v3) and complex shadow-query logic (CO-MOT), a genuinely useful design point for unified tracking.

Strong experimental coverage: results on four benchmarks (DanceTrack, BFT, AnimalTrack, MOT17), careful component ablations (proposal source, threshold, decoder depth, data scaling, denoising), and runtime analysis (20.7 FPS, shallow proposal pass) support the claims reasonably well.

The Track Attention Mass / normalized entropy diagnostic (Sec. 4.4) is a novel and interesting lens on query interference, inspired by attention-sink analyses in LLMs, and is complemented by cross-dataset analysis in the appendix showing the model adapts attention strategy to domain dynamics.

Honest reporting: the MOT17 results are presented candidly as below non-end-to-end SOTA, and the ablation clearly isolates the contribution of self proposals from training-data and denoising gains, which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: the core mechanism (injecting 4D anchor proposals into a MOTR-style decoder) is closely related to MOTRv2's detector-aligned anchors and the 'Anchor Proposal' variant in Tab. 1; the main delta is replacing the external frozen detector with a self-generated detection pass. The paper itself concedes the anchor-proposal variant is 'conceptually similar to [MOTRv2]'.

Headline results are competitive rather than clearly superior on the primary benchmark: on DanceTrack test SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) is slightly below CO-MOT (69.4) and MOTRv2 (69.9); the SOTA claim rests mainly on BFT (71.1), a smaller and less standard benchmark, and AnimalTrack where baselines are weaker.

The causal story linking attention statistics to the detection-association conflict remains correlational: Sec. 4.4 repeatedly uses 'we hypothesize' without an intervention experiment (e.g., explicitly regularizing attention mass) to verify that balanced track-attention causes, rather than merely accompanies, the gains.

The two-pass design doubles decoder computation per frame; while the shallow-proposal analysis mitigates this, a comparison of end-to-end tracking quality-vs-FPS against MOTRv2/v3 and CO-MOT under matched compute is missing.

Several aspects limit reproducibility and comparability clarity: the exact composition of the final model relative to the MOTRv2 stack (QIMv2, query denoising, CrowdHuman) makes it hard to attribute gains solely to self proposals on the test sets; no seed/variance reporting for main results; Fig. 2's caption and axis labeling are unclear (mAP values ~0.6 vs AP values of 66 elsewhere).

The 'fully end-to-end' framing is somewhat softened by the fact that the most effective prior-injection variant in the analysis (Tab. 1, Anchor Proposal, +6.8 HOTA) still relies on an externally pretrained frozen detector, and the self-proposal version recovers comparable but not identical gains on val (58.2 vs 58.0 HOTA, with a small AssA deficit).
No explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion; the MOT17 weakness is discussed but only in an appendix.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the paper empirically demonstrates the detection-association interference in MOTR-style joint decoders (Fig. 2 detection-only vs. tracking inference gap; Tab. 4a AP drop with track queries), which grounds the method in a genuine, previously reported phenomenon.

The proposed solution is simple and principled: reusing the model's own detection-only pass to generate 4D anchor proposals internalizes the external-prior idea of MOTRv2/v3, preserving the self-contained end-to-end character while removing the external detector. This is a sensible design point between MOTR and MOTRv2/MOTRv3.

Unusually thorough ablation section: four distinct prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) are compared (Tab. 1); proposal source (Tab. 7), threshold sensitivity, decoder depth (Fig. 6), runtime (20.7 FPS), and cumulative component analysis (Tab. 6) are all provided.

Broad experimental coverage across DanceTrack, BFT, AnimalTrack, and MOT17, with SOTA results on BFT (71.1 HOTA) and strong gains on AnimalTrack; results on the unfavorable MOT17 benchmark are honestly reported and discussed rather than hidden.

The Track-Attention-Mass and entropy diagnostic (Sec. 4.4, Fig. 5, Fig. 7) is a novel analytical lens adapted from attention-sink studies in LLMs, and adds interpretive value beyond the raw benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core mechanism (injecting detector boxes as 4D anchors into a MOTR-style decoder) is essentially MOTRv2's recipe with the external detector replaced by an internal two-pass forward. Similar decoupled proposal mechanisms exist in the detection literature (Deformable-DETR/DINO-style iterative anchor refinement) and in Co-MOT's shadow-query logic, so the contribution is closer to an engineering re-arrangement than a new modeling idea.

Attribution of gains over the MOTR baseline is confounded: the final system adds self proposals plus HSV augmentation, CrowdHuman pretraining, query denoising, and QIMv2. Comparisons against published MOTR/MeMOTR numbers, which lack these extras, overstate the benefit of the proposal mechanism itself; Tab. 4b/6 partially disentangles this, but the final DanceTrack gain over a properly matched baseline is not isolated.

On the primary benchmark (DanceTrack test), the method does not surpass the strongest end-to-end competitor (69.2 vs. CO-MOT's 69.4 HOTA, lower DetA), and remains behind the external-detector MOTRv2; the headline SOTA claim rests mainly on BFT, a comparatively niche dataset.

The attention-mass analysis is largely correlational and speculative: the paper repeatedly 'hypothesizes' that the observed attention imbalance causes the detection deficit, but no intervention (e.g., ablating track-query attention, reweighting attention) establishes causality between the diagnostic and the performance gain.

The dual-pass design doubles decoder computation per frame; while the shallow-proposal analysis mitigates this, complete end-to-end latency/FPS comparisons against MOTR, MeMOTR, and CO-MOT at matched hardware/settings are missing.

No qualitative results (tracking visualizations, failure cases) are presented, and reproducibility would benefit from details such as variance over seeds, which are absent despite multiple near-threshold comparisons.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the detection-association interference in joint end-to-end trackers (MOTR family) is a recognized issue, and the paper's central observation — that a strong latent detector exists inside MOTR but is suppressed during joint decoding (Fig. 2, Tab. 4a) — is a useful and reproducible empirical finding.

The proposed mechanism is simple, detector-free, and conceptually clean: self-generating proposals via the model's own detection-only pass removes the external-detector dependency of MOTRv2/v3 while preserving the benefit of explicit anchors. Table 7 convincingly shows self-generated proposals match frozen-detector anchors (58.2 vs 58.0 HOTA), directly validating the core design claim.

Unusually thorough ablation design: the paper systematically compares four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal, Tab. 1), isolates the contribution of each added component (Tab. 6), studies proposal threshold, decoder depth, data scaling, and runtime (20.7 FPS reported). This level of analysis supports the scientific case well.

The attention diagnostic (Track Attention Mass with cardinality correction, plus normalized Shannon entropy) is a genuinely interesting analysis tool, and the layer-wise context/synthesis phase narrative (Fig. 5, Fig. 7) offers a plausible mechanistic account of why the method works, extended across three datasets.

Evaluation spans four benchmarks, with state-of-the-art results among end-to-end trackers on BFT (71.1 HOTA) and AnimalTrack (45.5 HOTA), and honest reporting of the weaker MOT17 results in the appendix rather than hiding them.
Appropriate attribution throughout: the paper explicitly acknowledges similarities to MOTRv2, CO-MOT, and prior denoising/memory techniques, which strengthens scholarly credibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to MOTRv2/v3. The paper itself concedes (Sec. 3.1) that anchor proposals from a pretrained model are 'conceptually similar to [51]'. The core delta — generating the anchors internally rather than from an external detector — is well-executed but a relatively small architectural step, and the strongest single ablation gain (Tab. 1, +6.8 HOTA) comes from exactly the strategy the paper then abandons for its final method.

On the primary benchmark (DanceTrack test), SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) does not surpass CO-MOT (69.4) and trails MOTRv2 (69.9); the headline gains come from the less-standard BFT and AnimalTrack benchmarks. The abstract's 'leading with 71.1 HOTA on BFT' framing slightly overstates the overall competitive position.

Comparison fairness is a concern: a large fraction of the final performance comes from components borrowed from prior work (HSV augmentation, CrowdHuman joint training, QIMv2, query denoising — Tab. 6 shows 58.2→64.3 HOTA from these alone). The paper does not fully clarify whether all compared end-to-end methods use comparable training recipes, making the end-to-end table comparisons (Tab. 2) harder to interpret.

The causal claims from the attention analysis are somewhat loose. Track Attention Mass and entropy distributions are correlational diagnostics; the paper hypothesizes that 'balanced utilization of track context directly mitigates the detection-association conflict' but provides no interventional experiment (e.g., manipulating attention) to confirm the mechanism, and the MOTR baseline in Tab. 1 uses a different training setup than the anchor-proposal row, complicating exact attribution.

No variance/statistical significance reporting; several headline improvements over CO-MOT are within ~0.2 HOTA, so single-run results are difficult to weigh. Reproducibility would benefit from seed reporting or code release details beyond a project page.

The two-pass design roughly doubles decoder compute; while 20.7 FPS is reported, there is no latency/memory comparison against CO-MOT or MOTRv2 under identical hardware settings, and the sensitivity of performance to the proposal threshold is only studied at two values (Tab. 4c).

No discussion of limitations or societal impact in the main text; the MOT17 weakness is only addressed in the appendix. Given the paper's central claim of a 'default design principle' for unified tracking, a stronger treatment of where the approach does not help (crowded pedestrian scenes) would be appropriate.
